seo.title: Karmic tail 15 20 5 compatibility: the Devil, Judgement, Hierophant
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 20 5 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, Judgement in the middle, the Hierophant as the main task, read through the Hymn to Demeter.

title: Karmic tail 15-20-5 in compatibility: a pomegranate seed and the law a couple writes for itself
short: The card of the main task in a couple with the 15-20-5 tail carries a Greek name from Eleusis. There the hierophant was the priest who showed the initiates the sacred things of a rite. The rite was kept for more than a thousand years, and it was founded at the end of one family story: a bride is carried off under the earth, her mother stops the harvest, and then every side negotiates how the year will be divided. The three cards of the tail run in the same order as the three acts of that story. The Devil is a union that began without anyone being asked and holds tight. Judgement is the family, the walk out into the light and the union's second birth. The Hierophant is the law the couple has to write for itself rather than receive from its parents.

sections.h2: Why the couple's main task is named after a priest of Eleusis
paragraphs: The word "hierophant" is Greek: ta hiera, the holy things, and phaino, to show. A hierophant is "the one who shows what is holy". That was the title of the chief priest of the Eleusinian Mysteries near Athens, and the office was handed down inside one clan, the Eumolpidae. In the Marseille deck the card was called the Pope, and Waite lists its names: "The High Priest or Hierophant, called also Spiritual Father, and more commonly and obviously the Pope." But under the Greek name lies a Greek plot, and it is about a marriage.

The plot is told in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, composed in the seventh or sixth century BC; quotations here follow Hugh Evelyn-White's 1914 translation. The last scene of the hymn is the founding of that very rite. Demeter goes to the kings of Eleusis, and among them is named Eumolpus, forefather of the later hierophants: "she showed the conduct of her rites and taught them all her mysteries… awful mysteries which no one may in any way transgress or pry into or utter, for deep awe of the gods checks the voice" (ll. 474–479). The first hierophant of the hymn turns out to be the goddess herself: she "showed" the holy things, which is exactly what the card's name means.

So the card of this couple's main task is the last page of a story that opens with a bride being carried off. And before that last page the hymn passes through the same two cards that stand before the Hierophant in the tail: an underground kingdom and a return to the light.

There is no villain in the hymn and no wedding feast. There is a union made without asking, a mother who would not accept her son-in-law, and an agreement after which everyone is still alive. The 15-20-5 tail describes the same road: from a tether, through the judgement of the families, to the couple's own law.

sections.h2: A narcissus at the will of Zeus: the Devil at the entry to the task
paragraphs: The hymn opens with a trap. Persephone is gathering flowers in a meadow, and among them grows a narcissus "which Earth made to grow at the will of Zeus and to please the Host of Many, to be a snare for the bloom-like girl" (ll. 8–10). The Host of Many is one of the names of Hades. The girl reaches for the flower with both hands, the earth splits open, and the lord of the dead carries her off in his golden chariot.

No one asked the bride, and no one asked her mother. The father allowed it, the groom took her. The hymn tells this bluntly, as an abduction, and in the life of a couple with the 15-20-5 tail nobody steals anybody. But the pattern is recognisable. The union comes together fast and almost by itself: within a month they live together, within half a year they share a business, debts or a flat, and the relatives learn about it all once the decision has been made. Often one partner draws the other into their own world — their city, their circle, their routine — and the other follows with delight, as if reaching for a flower.

The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, and its common language. The Devil at the entry wants everything: to be a whole world to each other, with no room for outsiders. Such couples have an underground kingdom of their own — jokes nobody else gets, secrets they do not share, a tone of "us against everyone". On the site the same point also stands in the relationship line as "Common language", so for all these couples the Devil sounds there too.

At its best this is courage. The two are not afraid of each other's dark sides; they speak aloud about desire, jealousy and money — the things other households hide. Passion is not a matter of shame here. But the entry point sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. "Being everything to each other" slides quietly into "you're mine": where were you, why didn't you answer, what do you need those people for. What holds the two is no longer tenderness but closeness, money, a shared home. Wishes stop being spoken: why bother, it's obvious. Lisovskaya's closing thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple reads like an antidote to this entry: nobody belongs to anybody.

Who pulled whom into that kingdom first is the first argument of such couples. The hymn answers it unexpectedly. In despair the mother questions Helios, the Sun god who sees everything, and he replies: "None other of the deathless gods is to blame, but only cloud-gathering Zeus who gave her to Hades" (ll. 77–79). The one to blame is not the groom but the father who disposed of his daughter's fate. Benebell Wen writes of the Devil in almost the same words: the card "does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame… While the Seeker is not entirely innocent… the greater culpability rests elsewhere." In our reading, the chain at this couple's entry is most often forged before the couple exists: in parental homes where love was held in place by guilt, money or control. The two only bring it along.
If the tether has turned into surveillance, pressure or fear, it is no longer a question for the cards: a psychologist can help, and if there is danger, call a local emergency number.

sections.h2: The mother with torches: Judgement in the middle of the task
paragraphs: The second act of the hymn belongs to the mother. For nine days Demeter wanders the earth with a torch in each hand and eats nothing. Hecate heard the cry "yet saw not with my eyes who it was" (ll. 57–58). Only Helios saw, and he does not just name the culprit — he stands up for the groom: "Aidoneus, the Ruler of Many, is no unfitting husband among the deathless gods for your child" (ll. 83–84). Where the translation says "husband", the Greek has gambros, son-in-law. This is a family conversation about whether the daughter's husband is good enough.

The mother accepts neither the son-in-law nor the verdict. She withdraws from the gods and stops the harvest: "she vowed that she would never set foot on fragrant Olympus nor let fruit spring out of the ground, until she beheld with her eyes her own fair-faced daughter" (ll. 331–333). Embassies come to her with gifts, and she turns them all away. Then Zeus sends Hermes under the earth to "lead forth chaste Persephone to the light from the misty gloom" (ll. 337–338).

For Lisovskaya, Judgement is the energy of lineage and family: parents, traditions, inheritance, the way relatives accept a partner. For Waite and Wen, Judgement is a summons, a resurrection, a passage from one era of life to the next. In the middle of this tail both meanings meet in a single scene: the families call up into the light a union that has been living underground.

In real life this is recognised at once. The first holiday at the parents' house, where the partner is greeted as the one who "took our daughter away" or "took our son". The ultimatum "I won't come to the wedding until…". Relatives with presents and arguments. The demand to show themselves: register the marriage, introduce the families, do it "properly". A couple that has lived in its own secret kingdom finds itself in daylight for the first time, in front of everyone.

That walk into the light can be a second birth. Two people who have passed through the judgement of the families come out no longer as lovers whom people whisper about, but as a couple everyone knows and calls by name. But the middle of the task can also get stuck. One scene in the hymn describes that stuckness better than any analysis. Hermes finds Hades on his couch, and beside him sits his wife, "much reluctant, because she yearned for her mother" (ll. 343–344). Her body in the union, her heart in her parents' house. It happens in couples too: they live together, yet every decision is silently checked against mother; they quarrel with each other, yet the verdict comes from the relatives; they blame the partner without owning their own share.
Hades in this scene "smiled grimly" — in the Greek, he smiled with his brows (l. 357) — and obeyed. He has to let his wife go to her mother, and he does it without shouting. But with a gift.

sections.h2: A pomegranate seed: how the tether passes through judgement
paragraphs: Before letting Persephone go, Hades gives her a pomegranate seed: "he on his part secretly gave her sweet pomegranate seed to eat, taking care for himself that she might not remain continually with grave, dark-robed Demeter" (ll. 371–374). When they meet, the mother's first question is whether the daughter ate anything below, and she tells her to "speak out and hide nothing". A law hangs on the answer: whoever has tasted the food of the dead must go back, "there to dwell a third part of the seasons every year" (ll. 398–399).

The scene has two versions, and both are in the same hymn. The narrator says: he gave it secretly. Persephone tells her mother something else: "he secretly put in my mouth sweet food, a pomegranate seed, and forced me to taste against my will" (ll. 411–413). The same evening told in two voices is familiar to a couple in the middle of this tail. One is sure they imposed nothing; the other is sure they were presented with a done deal. The parents hear whichever version is brought to them.

The seed holds the mechanism of the whole tail. The Devil's hook holds only because there is a rule: she ate, so she is bound to return. Without the law the seed would be just a sweet. In a couple, too, a tether rarely rests on passion alone — it rests on rules that both families accept without discussion. Took money for the flat — the parents get a say. Accepted a present — must come and visit. One partner leaves for the holidays with their own family, and behind them comes the sigh, "of course, go". Each such seed is small and sweet, and together they decide who owns the year.

The task of the middle is for each partner to own their share. In the hymn nobody does: Hades keeps quiet about the seed, Persephone says "by force", the mother demands, the father decides. That is why the elders have to decide for the couple. Two people who can say "yes, I wanted this" and "yes, I agreed" take the decision back for themselves.

sections.h2: A third of the year: the Hierophant as the couple's main task
paragraphs: The last act of the hymn is an agreement. Zeus sends Rhea to Demeter — her own mother, Persephone's grandmother — and she brings the decision: the daughter will spend a third of the year under the earth and two thirds with her mother and the gods. "So has he declared it shall be and has bowed his head in token" (ll. 465–466). Demeter brings back the harvest and founds the mysteries. The world is saved, and every side has got what it wanted.

Every side except the couple itself. The agreement involves the father, the mother, the grandmother and the son-in-law, yet in the whole hymn Persephone never once says how she would like the year divided. The law of her marriage is written by the elders. This is the main task of the 15-20-5 tail read through its minus: a union whose rules were drawn up by the parents, by tradition, or by one partner on behalf of both.

It shows in the calendar. Whose parents get New Year. Summer at mother's country house, because "it's always been that way". How many Sundays a month belong to the families and how many to the two of them. Whose place to live in for the first years. Whoever provides the money gets their third. Among the tasks of a couple with the fifth energy, Lisovskaya lists living with the parents or on their support, relatives interfering even in the choice of a partner, conflict with the partner's family, and the difficulty of reaching a joint decision about the family. The hymn has all of it — only instead of a country house, there is the underworld.

The Hierophant has a second shadow, an inner one. This is lecturing: the wish to remake the partner, "we don't do things that way in our family", the right way to live that one person knows on behalf of both. Eleusis offers an image for it. In time a custom took hold there: once a hierophant entered office, people stopped using his own name, and for the rest of his life he was called by his title. A marriage in which two people live by roles — "son-in-law", "daughter-in-law", "head of the family", "the mother of my children" — and have forgotten how to call each other by name also gives up names for offices.

Wen writes a sentence about the Hierophant that fits every character in the hymn: "a person should never assume he or she knows better than another and therefore try to “protect” or shield someone else from knowledge. We are not the keeper of others." Demeter keeps her daughter, Zeus disposes of her, Hades keeps a secret. Three keepers, and not one of them asked the woman the agreement is about.

The good side of the fifth energy, for Lisovskaya, is a union where authority is accepted freely, where partners are also friends, where there are shared rules but personal space is respected, and where the couple creates its own holidays and places. The Hierophant is not the enemy of ritual. It is the enemy of a ritual the couple did not choose.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: Proserpina gives the law
paragraphs: The story has a sequel, and in it the roles change. Six centuries after the hymn, Virgil tells how Orpheus goes down for Eurydice. The rulers of the underworld let her go on condition that he does not look back — "for Proserpina had laid down this law" (namque hanc dederat Proserpina legem, Georgics IV.487; our translation). The girl who was once handed someone else's law now writes the law herself.

Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, adds a scene that every couple with this tail should know. Orpheus sings before the king and queen of the dead and reminds them of their own story: "and if the tale of that old abduction does not lie, Love joined you two as well" (X.28–29; our translation). The song moves them both, and they decide together: "neither the royal consort nor he who rules the depths can bear to refuse" (X.46–47; our translation). A union that began without asking is known, centuries later, as a union where two decide as two.

This is the strong version of 15-20-5. The tether of the entry becomes a choice the two repeat, now in the open. The judgement of the families stays behind as something passed through, not as permanent supervision. And the Hierophant of the main task is not a parental rulebook but a covenant the couple drew up itself and can revise, the way the seasons are revised. In Waite's divinatory list for the Hierophant, after marriage and alliance, there are also these words: "by another account, mercy and goodness". The law Proserpina gave was merciful: it let the dead go back to the living. But it had a condition. A good law for a couple is gentle too, but not empty.
What helps a couple through this tail:

ul: draw up their own calendar out loud and together: where the holidays go, how much time each family gets, what belongs to the couple alone; revise it once a year;
name the seeds — a present with strings, a debt, a sigh at the door — and say plainly what is really wanted;
in the story of "who pulled whom in", own their share and never present the partner to the relatives as the accused;
speak to the parents about the couple's decisions in one voice agreed in advance;
start a rite of their own — a holiday, a place, a habit that existed in neither family;
not bring each other up: the couple's rules are an agreement between two, not a textbook for one.

sections.h2: What Waite and Wen saw: a chain, a trumpet and a cornfield
paragraphs: On Waite's Devil two figures are chained to an altar, and he writes of the one exalted above them that he "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". The Hades of the hymn is exactly that: the lord of the dead who smiles with his brows and obeys his brother's order. In his divinatory list Waite adds a proviso to the Devil that matters for a couple whose union began "from above": it is "that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil". A beginning without asking does not in itself make a union bad.

Wen opens her description of the Devil with the words: "The Lovers from Key 6 are chained by a horned beast". For this tail the phrase is almost literal: each partner has the Lovers in their personal matrix, and the couple has the Devil at the entry (more on this in the numbers below).

On Waite's Judgement an angel sounds a trumpet and the dead rise from their tombs. In the hymn that return is not a one-off: the mother promises her daughter a return every year: "But when the earth shall bloom with the fragrant flowers of spring in every kind, then from the realm of darkness and gloom thou shalt come up once more to be a wonder for gods and mortal men" (ll. 401–403). This couple's Judgement is not a single day of sentencing but a walk into the light that repeats.

The couple's values in most of these unions are the Empress. On Waite's card "a field of corn is ripening in front of her", and he writes that the Empress is "the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life", while "the way which leads out therefrom, into that which is beyond, is the secret known to the High Priestess". A cornfield, a door into life and a way beyond it: in our reading, Demeter and Persephone on one card. There is testimony from the other side as well. Hippolytus of Rome, a Christian writer of the early third century hostile to the mysteries, reports that at Eleusis the initiates of the highest grade were shown "an ear of grain in silence reaped". If he is right, the hierophant at the climax of the rite showed the Empress's grain — the card of this couple's values.

sections.h2: The numbers of the tail: both partners have the Lovers, only the couple has the Devil
paragraphs: A run through every date since 1900 shows that the 15-20-5 tail occurs in about one couple in 176 (0.568%), 51st of the 97 couple tails. And all of these couples share the same arithmetic.

The couple's tail is built from only three combinations of personal tails: 6-17-11 with 9-3-21 (42% of such couples), 6-8-20 with 9-12-3 (37%), and 6-5-17 with 9-15-6 (21%). So the entry of one partner's personal tail is always the Lovers, and the other's is always the Hermit. The Devil at the couple's entry is their sum: 6 + 9 = 15. One person's wish to choose and the other's wish to withdraw together make a shared world for two, closed to everyone else.

Yet both partners have the Lovers. In one they stand at the entry of the personal tail; in the other, at the centre of the personal chart (79% of couples) or in the personal karmic task (21%). This holds for every such couple, without exception. The Devil, meanwhile, is absent from all the main personal points of both partners in 49% of couples. Two people, each with Lovers of their own, add up to a couple with a chain at the entry — the very picture with which Wen opens her description of the Devil.

The middle and the task are also assembled from two people. In 37% of couples the couple's Judgement is one partner's own personal karmic task (personal tail 6-8-20): what that partner learns alone, the couple goes through together in the middle of the road. In 21% of couples Judgement is built from the Hierophant in the middle of one personal tail and the Devil in the middle of the other: 5 + 15 = 20. And neither partner has the Hierophant as a personal karmic task: the couple's main task is built from Strength and the World, Judgement and the Empress, or the Star and the Lovers. The couple's law belongs to neither partner in advance — it can only be put together jointly.
The centre of the couple's matrix — the atmosphere, what is between the two when no one is watching — comes in two kinds for these couples.

ul: **The Wheel of Fortune — in 62.3%.** A cycle in which the seasons repeat: leave for one's family and come back, let go and welcome. Waite writes that behind the symbol of the Wheel lies "the denial of chance". A third of the year by agreement is not chance either but a rhythm.

**The Sun — in 37.7%.** No date has the Sun at the centre of a personal chart; it appears only in couples. And for this tail it is always built the same way: Death at the centre of one personal chart plus the Lovers at the centre of the other, 13 + 6 = 19. In the hymn the Sun is Helios, the only one who saw everything with his own eyes. Waite calls the Sun's light "the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light". A couple with the Sun at the centre has an atmosphere in which the secret of the entry does not live long.

paragraphs: The couple's values are the Empress in 55.6%, the World in 31% and the Hanged Man in 13.4%. The Empress is the cornfield and the home. Waite's divinatory list for the World includes "route" and "change of place": a union between two homes. For the Hanged Man it includes "trials" and "sacrifice". This is our reading, not a rule from the books.

The first partner (07.08.1976) has the personal tail 6-8-20 and centre 4. The second (19.03.1979) has the personal tail 9-12-3 and centre 6. Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22.

paragraphs: The chart shows how the tail spreads across the couple's matrix. Judgement stands twice: in the middle of the task and at the point that shows how each partner's status and success affect the union. For the first partner Judgement is their own karmic task, and in the couple it becomes the shared middle of the road. The Hierophant also stands twice — in the main task and at the way into money: the couple's rules begin with the rules of its wallet, and the question "who gives, and on what terms" is the central one here.

Lisovskaya suggests adding up repeated energies. Two Hierophants give 5 + 5 = 10, the Wheel that stands at the couple's centre. Two Wheels (the centre and "What fills") give 20, Judgement, which is also on the chart. Three cards of Justice give 24 → 6, the Lovers, and they stand at "Where it sparks". This couple quarrels about choice and makes peace through rhythm.

The couple's values are the Empress, and that is the second partner's personal karmic task. Each of the two brings their own personal task into the couple's tail: one brings Judgement, the other the Empress.

sections.h2: The 15-20-5 tail in a personal matrix is another calculation
paragraphs: The order 15-20-5 also occurs as a personal karmic tail: 4,661 dates since 1900 give it. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points: in a personal matrix the tail is worked out from one person's karmic task and centre, while in a couple every point is the sum of two people. The reading of one cannot be carried over to the other. There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 15, 20 and 5: in a couple these three cards occur only in this order.

ul: **Entry to the task — 15, The Devil.** What the couple wants together: to be a whole world to each other, with a secret and a language of its own. The pull is strong and fast, and it is easy to mistake closeness for ownership.

**Middle of the task — 20, Judgement.** What the couple goes through: the families enter the union. Relatives judge and summon, and the union comes out into the light and is born a second time — or gets stuck in someone else's verdict.

**Main task — 5, The Hierophant.** What to learn: to turn a tether into a covenant. Rules, a calendar and a rite of their own — instead of a timetable drawn up by the elders, and instead of lecturing each other.

intro: This is not a forecast and not a verdict. The tail describes a plot that two people recognise in themselves, and it shows where the way out lies.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 15-20-5 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's road from a strong, closed tether (the Devil at the entry), through meeting the families and bringing the union into the light (Judgement in the middle), to the main task — the Hierophant: turning the bond into a covenant with rules of its own instead of living by the code of the parents or of one partner.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not an outcome. The Devil at the entry gives the couple passion and courage, Judgement gives the union a second birth, and the Hierophant gives the ability to live by a shared law. There is one difficulty: that law is easy to hand over to someone else.

faq.q: Which partner is the Devil and which is the Hierophant?
faq.a: Neither. Every point of the couple is the sum of two people, and no card of the tail belongs to one partner. Sex plays no part in the calculation: either partner may pull the other into their world, and the voice of the family may belong to a father as easily as to either mother-in-law.

faq.q: How is the couple tail 15-20-5 different from the personal tail 15-20-5?
faq.a: In the calculation and the roles of the points. A personal tail comes from one person's date of birth, a couple's tail from adding two matrices, and its points mean something else: the entry to the task is the couple's shared wish, the middle is the road, and the main task is what the two have to learn together.

faq.q: How common is the 15-20-5 tail in a couple?
faq.a: About one couple in 176 (0.568%), 51st of the 97 couple tails. The centre of the matrix in such couples is the Wheel of Fortune (62.3%) or the Sun (37.7%), and the values are most often the Empress.

ul: draw up their own calendar out loud and together: where the holidays go, how much time each family gets, what belongs to the couple alone;
name the seeds — a present with strings, a debt, a sigh at the door — and say plainly what is wanted;
own their share in the story of "who pulled whom in" and never present the partner to the relatives as the accused;
start a rite of their own that existed in neither family;
not bring each other up: the couple's rules are an agreement between two, not a textbook for one.

unit.title: A law written by two

captions.M: Want to be a whole world to each other
captions.N: Pass the families' judgement and step into the light
captions.D: Write your own rules instead of the elders' law

unit.meaning: Your task is to turn a tether into a covenant: your own calendar and rules, not a law written by the elders.
